core_classification.analysis: Vinca’s “Je t’aime!” is primarily a desperate avowal presenting her love as true. Its description as part of an emotional eruption and as a cry analogous to “Adieu!” gives it some independently expressive force, though it remains intelligible chiefly as an intensely delivered avowal. The surrounding refusal of separation lends weak commitment-like resonance, but the core words do not clearly undertake a relational obligation.
core_classification.ambiguity: The main uncertainty is whether the farewell comparison establishes genuinely expressive/reflexive force or merely characterizes the intensity and valedictory circumstances of a truth-conditional avowal. Performative force is only weakly suggested by the adjacent claim that she can no longer leave him.

utterance_status.description: The narrator retrospectively reports Vinca’s earlier direct utterance while reproducing its exact words in quotation.

contextual_interpretation: Vinca utters the words amid tears, desperate confessions, and horror at an impending separation. The simile “comme on crie ‘Adieu!’” frames the declaration as a despairing, almost valedictory cry: she avows love precisely when their future appears unreachable and separation intolerable. Her accompanying “Je ne peux plus te quitter!” intensifies the attachment and provides limited commitment-like resonance, while the narration’s account of their lifelong bond supports the avowal’s sincerity.

evidence.quotation_or_description: “elle avait éclaté en larmes, en aveux désespérés”
evidence.supports: The declaration belongs to a sequence of desperate confessions, strongly supporting truth-conditional avowal and providing some evidence of expressive eruption.

evidence.quotation_or_description: “Elle avait crié: «Je t’aime!» comme on crie «Adieu!»”
evidence.supports: The exact utterance explicitly avows love; comparison to a farewell cry gives positive, though not decisive, evidence for expressive/reflexive force beyond mere emphatic delivery.

evidence.quotation_or_description: “«Je ne peux plus te quitter!» avec des yeux pleins d’horreur”
evidence.supports: The adjacent utterance situates the avowal within intolerable separation and supplies weak commitment-like or relational-undertaking resonance.

evidence.quotation_or_description: “L’amour, grandi avant eux, avait enchanté leur enfance” and Philippe “la chérissait”
evidence.supports: The narration presents their love as a longstanding relationship rather than an instrumental, rote, or semantically empty use of the formula.

ontology_assessment.diagnosis: T captures the central avowal, E captures the explicitly framed quality of a despairing emotional cry, and a small P score records limited commitment resonance. The valedictory and tragic framing is contextual nuance rather than a failure of the compact ontology.
